title: The bride's gift
hook: the mahr belongs to the bride

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nikah: consent of both, an offer accepted out loud, witnesses, a celebration. Your line was a contract of mercy. Where did you add a little mercy to the terms? Day one thousand two hundred eighteen.

A man stands up in the mosque in Medina. A woman has come to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and this man asks to marry her. The Prophet asks him: what do you have to give her? Nothing, he says, only this cloth I'm wearing. If you give her that, the Prophet says, you'll be sitting there with nothing on. Go and look for something, even an iron ring. The man goes. He comes back. Not even an iron ring. The story, in Sahih al-Bukhari, isn't over. But notice what's being searched for, so hard: something for her. Today's word: mahr.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU HAVE TO GIVE HER?` → `ONLY THIS CLOTH.` → `EVEN AN IRON RING.`

segments.voice: Mahr is the bride's gift, given by the groom, and it is part of the nikah from yesterday. First, what the Qur'an calls it. Surah four, verse four, in Pickthall's translation: "And give unto the women (whom ye marry) free gift of their marriage portions." A free gift. Not a price paid for a person, not a fee to her family. Second, whose it is. In Islamic law the mahr belongs to the bride. Not to her father, not to her brothers, not to the couple's shared account. Hers. The same verse goes on to say that if she chooses, of her own accord, to give some of it back, that's her call to make. And a little further on in that surah, the Qur'an tells husbands not to take back what they gave, even if it was a great amount. Third, the story from the hook. The man came back without even a ring. So the Prophet asked: what do you know of the Qur'an? The man named some surahs he knew by heart. And the Prophet married them for what he knew of the Qur'an. Some versions of the report say he was to teach them to her. The gift doesn't have to be gold. It does have to be hers. Fourth, how it's done today. Some couples agree a mahr paid at the wedding, some write part of it into the contract to be paid later, and the schools differ on details like whether there's a minimum. This week ran from schools to law in life: other schools, one row, why they differ, the fatwa, the judge, the nikah, and now the gift. By the end of it, the questions had turned into who owes what to whom.
screen: `A FREE GIFT, NOT A PRICE.` · `HERS, NOT HER FAMILY'S.` · `WHAT DO YOU KNOW OF THE QUR'AN?` · `PAID NOW, OR WRITTEN IN FOR LATER.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about a gift that is hers alone, or his, or theirs. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you love. Now think of something you could give them that would be wholly theirs. Not a gift that's secretly for you, not one that comes with a favor attached. It might be money. It might be time. It might be something you know and could teach them. Hold that gift in mind, and notice how it feels to give without keeping a share. If you pray, you can remember that person kindly in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Mahr. The bride's gift, given by the groom as part of the marriage. The Qur'an calls it a free gift, and it belongs to her. Today's word.
Your line: hers alone. Today, give someone one thing that is fully theirs, with nothing attached, not even a thank-you. Day one thousand two hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: In a Muslim marriage the groom gives the bride a mahr agreed in the contract, sometimes paid at the wedding and sometimes partly deferred; it belongs to her, and couples choose amounts from the symbolic to the substantial.

original.note: Arabic: the bride's gift, given by the groom and belonging to her.

trapdoor: what you thought: mahr is a bride price, a payment for the bride.
what it means: mahr is a gift from the groom to the bride, and it belongs to her alone.
what a scholar hears: the Qur'an's own word for it in 4:4 is a free gift; the schools differ over a minimum and over the portion deferred in the contract.
recall: a small tablet of baked clay

notes: Editor pass: week look-back ending changed from 'each time, the question was who owes what to whom' (not true of every day listed) to a narrower line.
Week end (1212–1218): look-back is folded into the end of the teach.
Qur'an 4:4 quoted from Pickthall; confirm exact wording. The rest of the verse (if she remits part of it of her own accord) is paraphrased.
Bukhari 5135 (also 5030, 5087 and others) paraphrased; confirm the number. 'Some versions of the report say he was to teach them to her': confirm.
Schools differ on a minimum mahr (e.g. Hanafi and Maliki set minimums; Shafi'i and Hanbali do not); no amounts given.
Ali and Fatimah's armor-mahr was taught in year 3 (day 778); this script uses a different report to avoid repetition.
